content: Boarding starts before you leave the dock, selecting the right crew.
Sailors - You need these to make the ship work. During boarding they do low damage but have good HP.
Musketeers - The highest damage dealers, but also the lowest HP.
Soldiers - Deal 2x the damage of Sailors but have a bit less HP.
Mercenary - Lowest damage (even lower than Sailors) but highest HP.

Note that Soldier and Mercenary share the same symbol. 

Each crew type also has a Cargo Capacity stat, this indicates how much cargo you can take after winning a boarding.

The crew are placed into their units, the size of which depends on the total ship crew. You can find the max stack size by hiring crew, say 20 soldiers and then adding more until a new stack is created. 

There are some strategies that deal with crew hiring to manipulate what stacks you have, such as having 2-3 Muskets to bait attacks or small additional stacks of sailors, musketeers, soldiers and mercenaries to create information overload, as shown below.

The basic crew setup for a ship is the required number of sailors, 1 or 2 stacks of muskets and the rest soldiers. My personal preference for musket stacks is to have 1 stack if your ship can defend 2 stacks, 2 stacks if you can defend 3 stacks.

Below is my setup for the Octopus. The stack size is 30, so it has 3 stacks of sailors, 2 stacks of muskets, 2 stacks of soldiers and a tiny misdirect unit of Mercs. 1 of each stack of muskets and soldiers is the ‘weak’ stack in that it has 20 crew instead of 30.

For beginners who are not confident in their ability in the boarding game, an alternative is to use all soldiers and no muskets. This removes the need to worry about defending and attacking with your own muskets and lets you focus on attacking the enemy. It is not as strong but will allow practice in boarding while reducing the risk of losing even though you had a 20 crew advantage.

content: There are some fundamental aspects of boarding that an understanding of makes the entire experience easier.

Attacks occur every 3 seconds and will deal damage according to the damage stat of all your available crew. Damage is split between all units being attacked. As such, attacks early in the battle deal more damage. As crew are killed, the damage your attacks deal will be reduced.

Defended units reduce the damage taken significantly. Thus a defended unit that is the only unit being attacked will reduce a significant amount of the total attack damage. A defended unit that is one of many attacked units will only reduce a fraction of the total damage of that attack.
Defended units have their attack damage significantly reduced. As such, defending muskets the entire time keeps them alive, but they don’t deal their devastating damage.
Damage does not carry over if you kill all targeted stacks. Thus if a stack is about to be killed, single targeting it wastes a lot of damage.

The crew are always lined up on the ship the same, it goes Sailors, Muskets, Soldiers, Mercenary. Thus if you are attacking Soldiers, always attack those closest to the Muskets (or Sailors if there are no Muskets). The last stack in line is most likely to be Mercenaries.

content:
At its core, I would summarize the key to boarding is knowing when to attack the enemy muskets and when to defend your own muskets. Muskets, being the highest damage dealers but easiest crew to kill, are very important to whether you win or lose close boardings.

Knowing when to attack enemy muskets, when to defend your own, when to undefend your own to maximize their damage output is actually complicated. There is no simple answer. Different players have different crews, the risk reward changes depending on how many crew you lead or trail by and everyone is also trying to predict what the other person is doing and trying to counter it. 

The strategy of boarding comes down to risk management. If you lead, protect your vulnerable muskets, attack conservatively. If you are behind, you have to take risks with undefended muskets, targeting easier to kill crew etc.

The basic strategy to minimize risk is to defend your muskets and attack the enemy across several units. Attacking only 1-2 unit stacks at a time increases risk, as a defended attack reduces a significant amount of damage.

The following situations assume the enemy is also running a stereotypical crew, i.e. a few stacks of sailors, 1-2 stacks of Muskets and the rest Soldiers. 

If you outnumber the enemy significantly, ie 20+ crew, it is very difficult to lose. Defend Musketeers, attack all of the enemy units at once. Attacking all enemy units, then removing the attack from any unit being defended. If the enemy switches what they are defending, simply swap that attack to another unit that was previously being defended. 

The idea here is to spread out attacks to minimize the impact of defending. Even if you are attacking a defended unit, the damage lost is minimal because you are spreading out your damage across so many units.

If you have a crew advantage of 10-20, the play is similar to above, but you have to be careful about enemy muskets. Wasting all your damage on defended muskets, or not attacking undefended muskets for multiple attacks will result in the enemy bringing back that gap.

If the difference in crew is less than 10 either way, this is where the game can be 50/50 if both players know what they are doing. If both sides have similar units, it comes down to who gets the best of musket attack and defend.

If you have a crew disadvantage of 10-20, you must take some risks to make up the difference. You still want to start off defending muskets, as taking a musket hit early on is brutal, but you are going to get in some musket attacks to make up that difference. Depending on the time left in the boarding, you may need to make some risky single stack attacks.
If you have a crew disadvantage of 20+, hope the person doesn’t know what they are doing, has a poor crew setup or falls asleep. Very little chance of winning against a competent boarder.

content: The very first step of creating builds is knowing your upgrades. I split them into 3 categories.
Offense are those that directly increase your damage output.
Defense is anything that directly increases how much damage your ship can take.

Technically Iron Ram could be put into Defense, but it is never really used for that purpose.

The last category is Utility, which is everything else. The secret last category is mortars, which obviously only come into play when dealing with mortar ships.
data.utilityRule: Everything else; the guide notes Utility can lean offense or defense and treats mortars as a specialist category.

content:
There is some nuance to Utility, since they can favour defense or offense. Something like Combat Arsenal can go either way depending on your consumables. 

Now onto actually creating a build.

Identify the core requirements of the build based on the role it is going to play. This includes identifying the cannons that can be used. 

Designate the 4 upgrade slots to the categories.

As an example, a long range kite build.  It needs speed and range, so Jericho’s with a focus on utility.

Since it needs to be utility focused, start off with 2x Utility, 1x Offense, 1x Defense.

Look through the Offense mods and identify what does and does not work for the role. 

You repeat the process for each upgrade slot.  

In the example of a long range kiting build, you come out with something like Reinforced Masts, Fortified Ports, Incendiary Mixture, Repair Arsenal.

After upgrades are consumables. The exact same process is followed. You have 3 slots, each consumable is either Offense, Defense or Utility.

Currently, Offense is largely ignored because the balance of consumables heavily favours Defense. 

For a kiting build we might want either 2x Defense, 1x Utility or 2x Utility, 1x Defense. For now let’s say we go with Large Sails, Smoke and White Double Powder.

The final area to fill out is crew. The easy way to do this is to start with the 3 you can’t go wrong with. Carpenter, Provost and Sub-Lieutenant. These are all strong crew members that fit on pretty much every build. The last slot can change depending on requirements. For a kiting build, Sail Handler for extra speed fits. 

If the build is more niche, say a boarding build, you can get rid of Provost so you have 2 slots open. Carpenter and Sub-Lieutenant are extremely strong though and hard to get rid of.

With specialist crew out of the way, you choose the main crew loadout. This is a choice between having some boarding crew, or going all sailors. If you are trying to avoid boarding, all sailors. 

For a kite build, all sailors, since we don’t want to ever be in boarding range.

So you put that together, go out and sail with it and see how it feels. Say after some fights you feel that most ships you are firing at are within range without Fortified Ports or White Powder. You can exchange Fortified Ports for something else, Combat Arsenal and the White Powder can be exchanged for Bronze Patches. 

Test and repeat as required.
Peace and Decoy Flags are flags to protect yourself from PvP. In WO we rarely use them, they are mostly for transporting valuable goods.

Faction Flag is the default PvP flag and the default flag you should use. There are also guild specific quests for Influence Points that can only be earned with PvP flags.

Faction Flags are where you also find the Tension-raising mode. See Tension for information on what this does.

No Flag is another PvP flag that you can unlock. It hides your name, guild and faction affiliations. It has a loot and XP debuff, so it's only used purely for PvP purposes. The main use for this flag is infiltrating enemy ports during attacks. When you are using this flag, enemy towers and forts take time to identification
Legendary Flag is a PvP flag that can be earned through the Arena. It comes with upgraded loot and XP bonuses. This flag does not allow any tension activity, so should not be used during RvR.

The goal of the game is to capture ports, the way you do that is through the Port Battle system. There are two phases, Tension and the Port Battle itself. 

Tension
Before a port can be attacked, it must have Tension raised to 100%. The only time this can occur is during a designated 2 hour window. Outside of those 2 hours, Tension can only be raised to 50%.

To raise Tension, the designated attacking guild must have players using the Faction Flag with Tension Mode on. They then sink Patrols (+5) around the target Port. Enemy players (+3) from the Guild that owns the port also count towards Tension, as do their Trusted Guilds (+1). 

The same occurs in reverse when attacking players are sunk. Sinking players (-3) from the attacking guild or Trusted Guild (-1) lowers Tension. Pirate NPS (-1) also lower tension.

Tension fights often involve larger alliances on top of Trusted Guild status, cross faction alliances, neutrals and 3rd parties. It is what it is, there is nothing that can be done about it currently.

When Tension reaches 100%, a Port Battle will be scheduled. It is an instanced battle that opens up 9 minutes after 100% is reached. The number of players and the ships that can be used depend on the port, with battles being 10v10, 15v15, 20v20 and 40v40.

40v40 battles are an exception in that they occur 24 hours after Tension is raised to 100%.

Guild leaders will select who is going into the battle and the ship composition. These players will sail out of the buoys when the Port Battle starts and enter the instance. The instance can be entered from anywhere around the port by pressing spacebar when prompted. 

Since the Port Battle instance entrance is a large area surrounding the port, everyone not selected to go into the Port Battle should have either sailed away or docked up. It is easy to join the Port Battle by mistake.

Port Battles use a ticket system, with ships sunk losing a team tickets. Attackers start with more tickets than defenders, but defenders have fortifications to assist them.

The goal of attackers is to destroy all of the fortifications and capture the Fort. The goal of the defenders is to either get the timer to 0, or sink all enemy ships when there are no tickets remaining. When attackers get down to 0 tickets, the timer will be set to 5 minutes.

Since tickets are lost by being sunk, the primary goal for inexperienced players is to not get caught out and sunk unnecessarily.

content: When a ship is sunk, it loses integrity. Ships have a maximum amount of integrity they can lose (often referred to as pips) before you have to repair them. Repairs cost Bronze, Canvas and Beams. The amount of materials required can be halved by using Gold (this should always be used).

Ships will have a repair time during which they cannot be used. For most ships, this time is a few minutes. The exception is the Octopus and Huracan, for which a full repair is measured in hours, not minutes.
Always select the ‘For resources and gold’ option when repairing

Allows ship swapping and repairs. Very useful.

Pretty obvious, it lets you store more stuff on the Private Island

Once you have a Private Island setup for crafting, you should not produce ship building materials in Ports. Instead your Port crafting should be used to turn Iron Ore into Iron, or excessive amounts of gold into chests to keep it safe. 

The main workshop in Ports that does get used is the Casting Workshop. This allows you to craft cannons, mortars and ammo.

content: Around the map there are various resource nodes that you can build mines/gathering facilities on. There are captain skills associated with these, such as increasing the number you can build up to 8 and allowing them to work without provisions.

Due to supply and demand from Ports, there are two main resource nodes used. These are Iron Ore and Wood.

Iron Ore is by far the most important initial resource as it is used in abundance for ship building.

You can turn Iron Ore into Iron at a Port using Port Hours and Coal. Making Iron is what most Port crafting hours are used for. 

Wood is a good secondary resource to collect, as it is required in large quantities. Not only do you constantly need it to use the repair ability, it is required to build Beams. After crafting all the ships you want, Beams become the primary product you need for repairs.

Coal is another resource that can be useful to have. While not strictly necessary because you can buy it, it does save gold.

It is important to have your resource nodes within 7000 units of your Private Island (you can right click and drag on the map to measure distance). This is the distance that the Mission building allows automatic pickup of resources to the Private Island.
Two resource nodes being used. Yellow means they are either not stocked with supplies to work at 100%, or the storage is full.

content:
You can’t go and sink the enemy if you don’t have cannons. For end game ships Heavy cannons are used. There are two types, crafted and Pirate.

There is no single best cannon. Different situations call for different cannons. As such, the initial goal is to get enough of each cannon type to outfit an Apostolov (and some spares).
There are 3 archetypes, Cannons, Long Cannons and Carronades.
Cannons - Fastest reload, but lowest damage. They provide a wide gun arc and have average accuracy and range.
Long Cannons - Longest range and slightly improved damage over cannons, but at the cost of reload. A narrow firing arc and good accuracy.
Carronades - The highest damage, but longest reload and shortest range. They have an average firing arc, but the worst accuracy.

content: There are crafted cannons and Pirate cannons. Crafted cannons, as the name suggests, are those you craft. Pirate cannons are purchased at Pirate Ports using Pirate Tokens. All cannons can also be dropped from ‘’Pirate squadrons carrying weapons’’ NPS.
Generally Pirate Cannons are the better option.
Heavy Cannons are used on 1st and 2nd rates. They are a priority to take part in end game combat.
Pirate Cannons
36-pdr Inrogs are cannons.

38-pdr Jerichos are long cannons.

48-pdr Colossuses are carronades.

There are also crafted Heavy Cannons. 

42-pdr Carronades are the exception to Pirate cannons being better. They are superior to Colossus unless fighting point blank range.

You need a set of all of these cannons so you can equip your largest ship with a full loadout. Different tactics require different cannons and as metas shift, different cannons are more favoured over others.
3rd and 4th rates use medium cannons. There are medium Pirate cannons as well. These are Admirals, Scorchers and Stormbringers.

content: Other than cannons, there are Mortars and Special Weapons.

Mortars range from 6in to 11in. Different ships have different sizes they can equip. Mortars are crafted weapons. Instead of cannonballs they use mortar rounds, there are Strike Rounds and Shrapnel Rounds. Strike Rounds can be purchased from the Trading House, but Shrapnel Rounds must be crafted with a Casting Workshop. 

There are also Heavy Mortars and Barrel Launchers. These are purchased with Pirate Tokens. There are no sizes for these weapons, their stats are based on the ship they are put on.

Heavy Mortars are high damage, long range and their shots slow down any ship hit with a “hull breach”. However, they require a ship to pull up sails for a few seconds before firing and they have a long reload.

Barrel Launchers use Fire Barrels as ammo instead of mortar rounds. A single barrel is used regardless of how many Barrel Launchers are fitted to the ship. They are similar to Heavy Mortars, but deal less direct impact damage. Instead they spread a large fire on the sea to deal damage.
There are two special weapons that can be crafted (they are in Medium Cannons for some reason). There are a handful of ships that can equip them to the bow.

Alchemical Fire - Referred to as the Flamethrower, it spews out a stream of fire from the front of the ship. It has a short range. It doesn’t require ammo, instead it can only fire for a short period of time before overheating.

Imperial Bombard - A weapon that fires 8 cannonballs at once. It essentially acts as powerful bow guns.

content: There is no one super ship that can be used in all situations. We use different ships for different situations. When a call is made for ‘what ships’, these are the ships being called for.
Heavy / 1st Rates
Apostolov is used for Port Battles, both the Tension stage and Port Battle itself.
La Royale is the 1st Rate Mortar ship.
Huracan is the dominant heavy ship.
Skirmish / 2nd Rates

Lighter in terms of armour and firepower, but faster and more agile. These ships are typically used in small groups, farming groups, solo or specific tactical applications when attacking enemy ports. 

These ships are typically used with a ‘survival’ mindset, where not getting sunk is the primary goal. You sail the edges of enemy formations, poking and prodding them looking for someone to make a mistake and sail into a bad position where they can be picked out and sunk.
Firestorm is the premium fast ship and one of the dominant skirmish ships.
Octopus is the other dominant ship in this category.
Ingermanland is the budget option to get experience with skirmish playstyle.

2nd Rate Waters

Redoubtable is the replacement Heavy.

Adventure is a replacement for the La Royale. 

Shen is a replacement for the La Royale.
3rd Rate Waters
Bellona is the standard Heavy for 3rd rate waters.
Azov is an alternative to the Bellona.
Shen is the Mortar ship of choice.
4th Rate Waters
Constitution is the Heavy for 4th rate waters.
Sparrow is a very powerful premium Mortar ship.
Red Arrow is also a strong premium ship.

content:
You need to know how to board. Enemies will learn if you are an easy board and they will target you. 

Other than the boarding itself, a vital component of battles is avoiding being boarded in a losing situation. Boarding is a very strong offensive action, it protects your ship, winning can recover crew and you recover HP. 

If you are in a ship that has lower crew than nearby enemy ships, you should avoid being in boarding range. The primary example of this is Huracans. The only ships that should pull up alongside enemy Huracans are Huracans.

content: Typically referred to as “The Fort”, if a guild owns a port the Fort has Guild storage that can be used to store and transfer resources. The Guild will be based out of one specific Port and that Fort will be the primary one used to store resources.
Certain resources, such as Blueprint Fragments and Escudo cannot be traded without a minimum cost. The Fort can be used to transfer these resources at no cost.

Enemy and Ally Ports also have Forts and depending on faction affiliation, it will fire at ships alongside the Towers around a Port.

Not to be confused with “Forts” when referring to Imperial Forts.

content: There is a specific ship upgrade that lets players steal gold, often referred to as “Chest”

It allows players to steal 5% of a player's gold by boarding and choosing to rob the enemy player. It also lets other players steal your gold if they board you and choose to rob. 

The context in which this is said is “I have chest” or “XYZ has chest”. This lets you know in a ganking situation to let a specific player board so they can steal gold, or to identify an enemy that is likely trying to board. 

You can protect your gold by storing it as chests of gold, a craftable item in port. These chests can be stored at port and opened when needed. You do lose 2% of your gold stored this way, but it is well worth it.

content:
The arena is a good starting point for PvP. It has small scale battles, often with low tier ships, that allows practice for the real thing. It is also one of the focal points of daily quests, which are the main source of battlemarks. 

The San Martin and Constitution are good starter ships for the Arena. The San Martin in particular is a 5th rate and allows the completion of one of the daily quests.

The Arena also has a shop that allows you to spend points you have earned by playing Arena on some useful things.

The arena is a good way to hone basic shooting and sailing skills. It is also the best way to practice boarding, with boarding being a strong arena tactic.

content: Trading Mission is described as a Trade Union guild ability that discounts shipbuilding and cannon crafting, boosts mines/factories within 3000 radius, and can let a qualifying town build one rate higher ships if the town is at least level 6.

The community post says Trade Mission discounts only crafting resources (beams, bulkheads, plates, canvas), not marks or imperials; one mission can last up to 7 days and multiple missions can run at once, limited to one per occupiable port.

A 2025 post describes shipbuilding discount inputs as a fixed 20% port-faction bonus, Trade Mission up to 12% by town level, and a fixed 10% seasonal discount, yielding a claimed 42% maximum when all are at max. This is stored as a dated community claim because the Ship Constructor spreadsheet itself uses a 25% same-faction term.

Community notes say non-guild members may be allowed to request a mission by paying 100,000 gold to the admiral (a guild practice, not an official game rule), and that an active Trade Mission could be used to pay 500 gold in that port to view auction listings of all ports.
An August 14, 2026 post says Trade Missions cost 40 influence and 40 chests for each mission being opened.

content: Pirate weapons are presented as an alternative to crafted bronze weapons; the supplied notes describe them as higher-damage/slower-reload options that require Pirate Tokens and purchase at a Pirate Port Pirate Shop.

Pirate Tokens can be obtained by attacking Pirate Barons (starred pirate NPS). The guide recommends the southwest/left-lower map area, targeting 1–4 star pirate ships and even Santisima groups, and notes packs of 2–3 may appear.
The supplied farming observations say premium-account kills can yield roughly 35–75 tokens depending on HP/damage contribution, with 4000+ HP ships preferred. Groups of 2–4 are recommended.

The author reports 50–80 pirate chests (25k–39k gold) per hour and 200–600 tokens over the described farming sessions, explicitly depending on RNG/group conditions. Loot aboard a ship is said to be divided among players who dealt at least 300 damage.

Time-specific monetization examples in the notes: Inrog around 30k, Jericho around 40k each, Colossus around 50k, with Gray Island, Freedom Bay, St John and Devios cited as popular markets. These are observations, not canonical current market prices.

Named after the Mayan god of wind - Huracan, this giant is a symbol of the Inhagger Empire's military might, a native civilization whose technological level rivals and often surpasses that of the Archipelago states.

This ship was funded by the people of Cantabria ("the mountain" region of Spain, hence the name Montañés - "the Highlander"). It became the benchmark for later Spanish 74-gun ships of the line of the late 18th century. It took part in almost every major naval engagement from the late 18th to the early 19th century.

A warship built by the Empire's shipwrights. It was first captured during a battle with the Cult of the Witnesses of the Apocalypse. According to the dying captain of the cultists, these ships were found drifting crewless somewhere in the Endless Sea.
A famed French ship of the line that duelled with HMS Victory during the Battle of Trafalgar. The fatal shot killing Vice-Admiral Horatio Nelson was fired from this very ship.

Originally a French ship of the line, she was captured by Englishmen during the "Glorious First of June" battle in 1794. She served actively in the Royal Navy until 1807, participating in several engagements and capturing enemy vessels. In 1807, she was converted into a prison ship.

data.historicalInspiration: The "turtle ship" served as the core of the Korean fleet during the 16th and 17th centuries. In addition to her unique covered design, she wields combined armament, including mortars.

Line ship commissioned by Cardinal Richelieu as part of the naval reinforcement program. Participated in several battles and ultimately burned during the Battle of La Hougue after being attacked by English fireships.

The renowned British 50-gun ship of the line of the Portland class. Launched on April 24, 1790 in Portsmouth. Became a symbol of British naval supremacy after the incident with the frigate Chesapeake. A reliable veteran of the Napoleonic Wars, capable of enduring a prolonged duel. Met her end on June 28, 1814, wrecked in dense fog near Anticosti Island in the Gulf of Saint Lawrence.

Constructed in 1681 with private funds by Charles Mordaunt, Earl of Peterborough, and named after him. The ship was too heavily armed for a private vessel, leading to its confiscation in 1683. After legal battles, it was later purchased by the Royal Navy.

Named after the victory over the Swedish Empire at the Battle of Poltava, she was the first ship of the line to be laid down and built at the Saint Petersburg Admiralty. She features a "Dutch" transom and sculptures of Saint George as its decoration.

A 17th-century East Indiaman, belonging to the Dutch East India Company and the largest ship in their fleet. Her maiden voyage to the Dutch East Indies was in 1651. After several voyages, she sank near Madagascar in 1662. Fortunately, her blueprints are still in the hands of local shipwrights.

Originally a 17th-century Spanish Manila galleon, heavily armed and used to transport Spanish treasures from the Philippines to Mexico. After arriving in the Archipelago, the ship was redesigned and earned widespread fame.

profile.Faction: Kingdom of Kai and Severian Union

data.historicalInspiration: Main combat ship of the Kai fleet. Has a fearsome appearance, sturdy hull, hybrid armament and mortars, allowing it to fight in any conditions
One of the fastest and best-armed ships in its class, making her a formidable opponent for medium frigates.

One of the original six frigates of the United States Navy, the "Constitution" was larger and more heavily armed than its contemporaries. She gained fame during the War of 1812 against Great Britain, earning the nickname "Old Ironsides" and the adoration of many.
The "Devourer" is an Imperial ship with heavy armament on both the bow and stern. Its thick hull offers excellent protection, while jibs ensure good maneuverability.

A heavily-armed American frigate. It served in the First Barbary War and the War of 1812, where it captured 13 whaling ships during a single cruise. Later captured by the British, the "Essex" went on to serve under the British Crown.

Originally designed for trade expeditions and provisioning cities with its massive hold, this ship can also hold its own in combat. It gained an unfortunate reputation as a slave transporter during the height of the Atlantic slave trade.

Clippers are vessels with the most powerful sail rig and a unique hull design that minimized water resistance at the cost of maneuverability. This ship held the record for the fastest passage between New York and San Francisco - 89 days and 8 hours.
German "great" frigate of the 17th century. On July 25, 1692, the Friedrich Wilhelm departed Emden for Guinea. During the voyage, it defeated a French vessel.

First built by Maurice "Shipwright" Fleury in the port of Aruba. After falling victim to a plot by the Levenhook brothers, Maurice was tragically executed. In his memory, a skeleton holding a chalice - a symbol of grief - and a spear - a symbol of revenge - adorns the bow.

Tartanes were widely used across the Mediterranean - from Turkey to Spain - for a variety of tasks. They were especially favored by Algerian corsairs. Upon reaching the Archipelago, the tartane became popular with local pirates, particularly after Tortuga craftsmen fitted it with mortars.

The French ship Unite was captured and commissioned into the Royal Navy as HMS Surprise. She was considered a hybrid between a corvette and a frigate. The Surprise became famous in 1799 when she recaptured HMS Hermione from the French.

This ship belonged to the large and successful "Slava Rossii" class of ships of the line (built from 1733 to 1774 in St. Petersburg and Arkhangelsk; 58 vessels in total), known for their seaworthiness, maneuverability, and stability. "Three Hierarchs" was one of the key ships of the first major ocean expedition of the Russian fleet from the Baltic to the Mediterranean, and a symbol of the Chesme victory.
Norwegian gunboat schooner, one of ten built for the Dano-Norwegian fleet before the end of the Napoleonic Wars, when Norway became independent from Denmark under the Treaty of Kiel in 1814.
The combat galleon of the pirate prince Morgan Black, rumored to have been gifted to him by the Empire for his service. It's one of the best-armed ships of its class.

The "Black Wind" has a sturdy hull and can accommodate a large crew, providing solid protection in battle. However, this comes at the cost of a reduced cargo hold, making her less suitable for trade or prolonged engagements.

Originally a Dutch fluyt, it underwent significant redesign after arriving at the Archipelago. Many mistake it for the lightly armed "Friede", only to realize their error too late as mortar shells tear through their decks.

data.historicalInspiration: A Korean ship with a distinctive armored deck resembling a turtle shell, hence its name "turtle ship." The first of these ships fought the Japanese fleet at Sacheon. Local shipwrights further refined the design.

data.body: The crew performs many roles: loading cannons, managing sails, and fighting during boarding. The crew members are divided into sailors and boarding parties. You can hire crew members in any ratio, but a lack of sailors results in penalties to cannon reload speed and sail handling. Keep in mind that crew members often die during firefights. Special crew members provide unique benefits to the entire ship. Each has a limited service term and demands extra pay. These cannot be hired in ports but can be found in taverns , rescued at sea, obtained from captives , or recruited on personal islands . When traveling through port taverns, specialties depend on the type: cities feature soldiers and sailors, while pirates are found in pirate coves and pirate-controlled cities. Recruitment chance depends on the ship; higher in special modes. Recruiting on personal islands introduces rarer individuals compared to taverns.

Swivel guns fire using a separate button (default [Q]). They lack precise aim, so fire by approximation. Barrels and mines are close-combat tools to evade pursuers but can harm your ship if mishandled. Fireships are boats with powder charges targeting a selected ship. They can be destroyed by enemy fire, even at launch, causing full damage to your ship. So, pick carefully the moment to send them out.

# Shipbuilding

Ships are the main way captains travel, fight, trade, and interact with the world. New ships become available as you progress through the ship development trees; the starting fleet includes the Pickle and Friede.

## Building in the right port

Most ships belong to a shipbuilding school. Building a ship in a port aligned with that school reduces the required crafting materials by **25%**. Ships without an affiliated school do not receive that school discount.

## Core ship statistics

- **Durability** — how much punishment the ship can take before sinking. Higher durability also means more expensive repairs. Sail durability is tied to the ship's overall durability.
- **Speed** — the ship's maximum combat speed. Sail settings trade speed for maneuverability, and both upgrades and cargo load can affect performance.
- **Maneuverability** — how quickly the ship can turn at its standard combat sail setting.
- **Broadside armor** — reduces incoming cannon damage. Angling increases the effective thickness; the bow is sturdier and the stern is less protected.
- **Hold** — the maximum weight of cargo and equipment the ship can carry.
- **Crew** — the number of people available to operate the ship, load guns, perform actions, and fight in boarding. Larger crews are harder to disable or overcome in boarding.
- **Hull size** — larger ships are easier targets to hit.
- **Displacement** — heavier ships accelerate and maneuver more slowly. Ramming effectiveness depends heavily on both speed and mass.
- **Integrity** — decreases after a sinking in the open world, excluding Port Battles. When integrity is exhausted, the ship needs a major repair.

## Rates

Ships are grouped from **Rate I through Rate VII**. A higher rate is not automatically the best choice for every job. Progressing weapons, upgrades, and the ship trees is often more useful than simply chasing the highest-rate hull.

## Ship classes

- **Fast** — mobile ships built for ranged fighting, scouting, and support. They reward careful handling and punish mistakes.
- **Combat** — versatile ships suited to line fighting and agile attacks without an extreme strength or weakness.
- **Transport** — cargo-focused ships whose combat role is secondary.
- **Heavy** — durable, heavily armed ships intended for line fighting, defense, and positional combat, at the cost of speed and agility.
- **Siege** — nimble but fragile ships equipped for mortar work against forts, coastal defenses, and stationary targets.
- **Imperial** — ships captured from the Inhagger Empire; this is an origin classification rather than a single combat role.

Use the **Ships** article for the current fleet table and the **Ship Builder** when you want to fit a specific hull.

# Boarding

Boarding is close-quarters combat between ship crews. A successful boarding can let the winner loot the enemy, take crew, or capture the ship when the game allows it.

## Starting a boarding

Boarding becomes possible after the enemy has been weakened and the ships are brought close enough together. When the boarding prompt appears, the default control is **Space** to begin the boarding action.

## How boarding damage works

- Boarding attacks resolve every **3 seconds**.
- Your available crew determines the attack damage.
- When you attack several enemy groups, that damage is split between the groups being targeted.
- As crew are killed, later attacks become weaker because fewer crew remain available.
- Defending a group sharply reduces the damage that group takes, but it also reduces the damage that defended group contributes to your own attack.
- Excess damage does **not** carry over after every targeted group has been killed, so overcommitting damage to a nearly defeated group can waste an attack.

## Crew types

- **Sailors** — required to operate the ship. In boarding they have relatively low damage and good health.
- **Musketeers** — the highest-damage boarding crew, but also the most fragile.
- **Soldiers** — stronger attackers than Sailors with somewhat less health.
- **Mercenaries** — the toughest crew type in the guide, but with very low damage.

Soldiers and Mercenaries use the same symbol in the boarding interface. Crew types also have a cargo-capacity value that affects how much can be taken after a successful boarding.

## Crew order and targeting

Crew groups are arranged in a consistent order: **Sailors → Musketeers → Soldiers → Mercenaries**. That ordering can help you infer which groups you are targeting.

The central boarding decision is usually whether to attack the enemy's Musketeers and when to defend your own. Musketeers can swing a close fight because they deal heavy damage but die quickly when exposed.

## Practical strategy

A conservative setup uses the required Sailors, one or two Musketeer groups, and fills most remaining space with Soldiers. Beginners can simplify the fight by using Soldiers instead of Musketeers; it is weaker overall, but it reduces the number of attack/defend decisions while learning.

When you have a large crew advantage, protect your vulnerable Musketeers and spread attacks across several enemy groups so one defended target does not absorb most of your damage. With a smaller advantage, watch enemy Musketeers carefully and avoid wasting repeated attacks into defended groups.

When crew counts are close, timing Musketeer attacks and defenses becomes especially important. When you are behind, recovering the fight generally requires more risk: exposing your own Musketeers for damage or committing to narrower attacks at the right moment.

## After the fight

The available post-boarding choices can include burning the defeated ship for loot, taking some of its crew, or capturing the ship when there is room in your fleet.

Boarding is a risk-management fight: protect your highest-value crew when you are ahead, and accept more exposure when you need to recover a crew deficit.

data.body: Weapons are the primary offensive tools used in World of Sea Battle . They determine a ship's combat effectiveness through penetration, range, reload speed, accuracy, and special firing properties. Weapons come in different types, tiers, and categories, allowing players to customize their ship for various combat roles. Overview Weapons define how a ship performs in battle. Each weapon has unique characteristics such as penetration, loading time, angle of fire, and accuracy spread. captains progress through several weapon tiers, from basic cannons to elite pirate gear, either by purchasing, crafting, or acquiring them as loot. Weapon Tiers Weapons are divided into three major tiers. Basic Weapons Basic Weapons are the entry-level tier. Purchased directly for . Require no crafting materials. Ideal for early-game combat and low-rate ships. Often have simple stats and predictable performance. These weapons include most low-caliber cannons, early long cannons, and standard artillery pieces. See: Basic Weapons Advanced Weapons Advanced Weapons represent upgraded and specialized equipment. Must be crafted using gathered and refined materials. Require multiple components and . Provide improved stats over Basic Weapons . Often include better accuracy and/or faster reloads. Crafting allows captain's to tailor their ship's armament toward specific roles. See: Advanced Weapons Pirate Weapons Pirate Weapons are the most powerful weapons out there. They can be obtained through: Purchase using . Weapon convoys. Modes. These weapons generally outperform Basic and Advanced tiers in terms of pure damage. See: Pirate Weapons Weapon Types Weapons come in several categories, each suited to different combat strategies. Cannons Standard short- to mid-range artillery with balanced performance. Long Cannons High-range cannons with improved precision. Carronades Short-range, high-damage weapons that excel in close combat. Bombards Specialized weapons for bow and stern. Mortars Devastating damage against ships and perfect against forts and defenses. Special Weapons Exotic or unique weapons that may have special firing behavior or effects. Full article: Weapon Types Weapon Stats Weapons are defined by several statistics that affect their performance. Penetration/Damage - Determines damage output and ability to pierce hulls. Loading Time - Time required before the weapon can fire again. Range - Maximum effective firing distance. Max Angle - Maximum horizontal aiming angle. Accuracy Spread - Determines shot deviation. Full explanation: Weapon Stats Explained Acquisition Weapons can be obtained in several ways. Purchased for ( Basic Weapons) Crafted using materials ( Advanced Weapons ) Purchased using ( Pirate Weapons) Looted from Weapon Convoys ( All Weapons ) Earned in special game modes ( All Weapons) This progression allows players to upgrade their combat capabilities over time. Usage and Tactics Different weapon types reward different play styles. Cannons - versatile and reliable in most situations. Long Cannons - ideal for long-range engagements. Carronades - powerful in close quarters. Mortars - perfect against structures. Combining multiple weapon types can create interesting hybrid loadouts. Successful boarding allows you to capture NPS ships into your fleet. Their main roles are escorting, assisting in battles, and transporting cargo. Commands can be given to the fleet via the menu after pressing [Z]. Allied NPS ships can be repaired and dismantled in ports (yielding wood and cloth). During arena battles, other modes, or when you're offline, they wait in port. If your ship sinks or strays too far, NPS ships will lose command and await your return.

Cruise mode is when the ship gains a speed bonus under full sails. Fast ships gain bonuses quicker, but against the wind, bonuses don't apply. Use a spyglass to observe distant activities. Visibility drops at night or in bad weather, and depends on the ship size. Rivers and canals have currents that increase speed, even against the wind.

Flags define playstyles, activate or remove PvP protection, grant XP and loot bonuses, and allow access to certain ports. PvP protection does not work in the center of the map (inside the red circle) and in the Endless Sea. While under PvP protection, when multiple players sink a NPS, loot splits proportionally by damage dealt, or players compete for the entire loot.

The most dangerous phenomenon is a storm. As you approach the storm's center, you'll face squalls, heavy rain, and large waves. Wind in storm zones grants a speed bonus . Avoid dangerous listing during storms by furling sails on time or using upgrades. In cold regions, the crew requires additional provisions to survive, or they will perish. However, here no goods spoil, and you can find more resources and fish. In other regions, hunger levels will never reach critical values, but additional provisions provide a bonus .

Almost all resources are harvested or produced by players: from building materials to food. Resources can be traded with ports, but Trade House prices depend on quantity . Only other captains influence quantity. Profit from price differences by transporting between ports. At the Auction , captains trade goods, ships, and weapons. Port owners earn a commission from such deals. Items have unique traits; find efficient ways to trade them instead of selling at the first opportunity. Goods are special items transported and sold in regions where they aren't produced, earning higher prices.

At sea, you can find trading ships and various settlements. Their offers are unique and change daily. These traders sell ammo and provisions and offer profitable deals for buying and selling. In the Endless Sea, traders' offers are even more lucrative.

Mines are Production Sites located on various islands throughout the archipelago. They are one of the main sources of ores used for shipbuilding, trading, and crafting. Mines can be captured and upgraded by any captain, making them a vital part of regional economy and territorial control. Overview Mines are stationary Production Sites that continuously extract resources once owned and maintained by a player. There are currently four types of mines operating across the archipelago: Coal Mine – produces , used for smelting and trading. Copper Mine – produces , used for weapon crafting and refined into . Iron Mine – produces , used for shipbuilding, crafting and refined into . Ice Mining – produces , essential for port upgrades. Each mine consists of four levels , each increasing both production output and storage capacity. Higher levels also require additional materials such as and to upgrade. Exact output values differ for each mine type and can be viewed on the respective pages. Capture and Ownership Mines are neutral or player-controlled island buildings. To take control of a mine, a captain must approach the island and pay for the first level. Once purchased, the mine becomes owned by the captain and will automatically begin producing its respective resource at the rate defined by its level. Provision consumption Starting from Level 3 , mines consume to maintain active production. The higher the level, the greater the consumption rate. If provisions run out, production will pause until restocked. Worker bonus Assigned workers can increase the mine's efficiency, boosting hourly output. Strategy Mines are a steady and reliable source of resources, especially when upgraded to Level 4. Remember that Level 3 and 4 mines require to stay operational. Regularly collect produced ore to prevent warehouse overflow — once full, production halts. Secure multiple mine types to ensure a balanced resource supply chain for ship construction and port upgrades. Lore Mines have existed since the earliest settlements of the archipelago. and veins were the backbone of early naval industry, their fusion into giving rise to stronger ships and superior weaponry. powered the great forges of the era, while from deep ice caverns sustained ports and crews across the seas. Controlling mines has always meant power — both industrial and military — in the endless struggle for dominance over the archipelago. Every guild has a vault and a treasury The vault consists of chests, which can be voluntarily contributed to by members. It is used to pay for various services, including fortification upgrades, contracts, and investments. The treasury is used for payouts to members and is replenished from external sources. It is managed by those with the proper rights: the leader or first mate, by clicking on a member's nickname (including their own). Gold enters the treasury as taxes from captured cities. A part of this gold is immediately paid as salary to members, while the rest is deposited in the corresponding fort. Only after the port battle window is completed is the accumulated gold transported to the guild's treasury. At other times, it can be claimed through capture or plunder. In Arab cities, gold is directly deposited into the treasury.

You can grow your wealth (gold and resources) through these primary methods: Gathering : finding and collecting items at sea, exploring islands, and charting the map. Sinking ships: earning gold and resources. Boarding ships: gaining additional resources. Capturing and dismantling ships: yielding a large amount of wood and cloth. Fishing : use tackle to catch fish, which can be used for sustenance, sold, or traded for items. Trading : buy low and sell high. Prices are visible on the map and in trade houses. Sea traders: often have lucrative offers. Auction : find profitable deals or sell resources. Crafting : create in-demand goods, ships, or cannons, and sell them on the auction. Arena : earn Battle Marks that can be sold if surplus. Quests and missions: complete combat quests and deliveries from port taverns to gain scrolls and reputation as bonuses.

Most ports are towns and settlements on Archipelago islands, contested by factions. Cities are more developed, offering guilds the ability to impose mooring fees. Some ports belong to the neutral Coastal Brotherhood. This organization studies the Cataclysm's causes and effects while helping "newcomers" from beyond the sea adapt.

Controlling ports expands faction territories, generates income, produces resources, and collects taxes. All military actions require raising tension . Once it reaches 100%, battle entry becomes available, marked on the map. This occurs only during battle windows set by the port owner. At other times, tension caps at 50%. Each fleet in battle has its own respawn points - outposts. The goal is to destroy all towers and the fort, then land your infantry within the given time. Each destroyed object or ship extends the time limit. The maximum fleet size is 20. If the battle ends, your fleet's positions will remain occupied. Make sure to stock up on ammunition in advance, as ship integrity in these battles is not lost . Each fleet has respawn points based on the number of participants. Sinkings reduce the number of points, and when they are depleted, the fleet is removed from the game. Depending on their rate, ships subtract between 2 to 7 points, while heavy ships subtract between 4 to 9. The guild can use various options for timed protection , which does not allow for the increase of tension. But, these and any other actions, like repairs, cannot be activated, if there is any tension present. Capturing ports allows you to control regions, develop cities, and collect taxes and mooring fees. You can only attack ports belonging to enemy factions.

As a city develops, it grows larger and provides more bonuses to its owner and allied guilds. For military factions, allied guilds include all guilds, but for pirates, only trusted ones are included. A trading guild can open trade missions to receive bonuses by paying a fee, which depends on the city's level. It must pay regularly to maintain the mission. Allied guilds must make mandatory contributions to receive bonuses. This encourages factions to develop cities together.

After the port battle becomes available, the attacking guild will be able to rob the fort by destroying it. Compared to capturing it, you do not need to destroy any towers. You will be able to take resources from storage and receive a construction license . Warning: when robbing bays, you can only get 1 license. Raiding will decrease your respawn points, and each player who takes resources will leave the port battle. Therefore, it might be better to avoid risks when you have the chance to reclaim the port.

Fighting captains at sea is a chance to loot them, earn Battle Marks and experience, complete missions, and enjoy the thrill. Reputation affects faction city bonuses and outcomes when sinking players. Red players: pirates or those with bad relations with your faction. Sinking them is lawful and earns rewards. Yellow players: those with neutral relations with your faction. Sinking them may result in penalties. Green players: your allies or players with good relations with your faction. Sinking them may result in severe penalties. In port battles, the Endless Sea, or if attacked first, sinkings do not affect reputation. Black Marks are earned by sinking neutral players or ships with a significant rank difference. Military faction players receive a reputation penalty instead of a mark.

The higher the hazard level of the waters, the more high-rate NPS, better mission rewards, and more loot you can gather from islands and at sea. However, such zones are much more dangerous. There are shallow waters at sea, restricting access for ships of certain rates. For some, this is a limitation, but for others, it's protection from large ships. You may also encounter reefs that damage ships upon passage. The higher the speed, the greater the damage.

Many NPS ships play an important role in the economy, despite being frequently sunk for profit. Sinking NPS ships in daylight , especially traders , increases your notoriety level! It decreases over time. As your notoriety level rises, ships will attack you more frequently, and over time, bounty hunters will appear.

Raising tension can affect the port's economy and options that the controlling guild has, and can be used as a separate measure of influence Starting at 15%, the guild cannot issue decrees, including protection or window changes. At 30%, production efficiency decreases, and beyond that, tax income stops. Tension rises under faction flags. Multiple guilds can compete for tension, taking points from each other. To decrease tension , you need to sink pirate NPS under flags, or players that are raising the tension. In case of resource shortages, city tension slowly rises up to 100%, after which a revolt occurs, causing the guild to lose control over the port.
A guild is a large organization within a faction with its own hierarchy

Influence points are the primary "currency" for development, spent on guild upgrades, captured city enhancements, and increasing member limits. The main way to get them is by completing influence missions . All members of the guild contribute to the completion of the mission with their actions. The more developed the guild is, the harder the missions will be. Influence points earned during a season are displayed in the rankings. Spending points does not decrease your ranking.

Consumables can repair, enhance ship stats, or provide allies with bonuses. Defeating NPS or players can reward random consumables in an extra temporary slot. As with upgrades, creating combinations with consumables effectively leads to better results.

Ammunition and resources have weight , so choose carefully what to carry. Ammo and equipment are stored in a shared warehouse accessible at any port, but resources are stored locally, occupying space. Warehouses for resources have a weight limit. The limit can be increased by upgrading your warehouses, but the amount of upgraded warehouses is limited. You'll have to decide where to build or dismantle them.

NPS (Non-Player-Ship) are game-world ships. They can trade, gather resources, do seaway robberies and explore new sea routes much like any other player. A "red spyglass" over the name means the NPS may attack upon approach. Many NPS are vital to the economy, despite being targeted for loot. Sinking them can increase your wanted level and attract attacks, even from ships without "red spyglass."

Locals say a cataclysm years ago severed ties with the outside world. Only the Endless Sea remains visible where great nations once stood... You can go beyond the map to explore new territories, but it's highly dangerous.

In the crafting section, you can process raw materials (like ore) into resources, which are then used to create craft resources (such as bulkheads, sailcloth, plates, bronze) for building ships and upgrades. This requires craft - time , which regenerates over real time. Skills affect its limit and respawn rate. To craft components, you'll need to unlock a specialty workshop . You can have up to two of the Specialty Workshops as you level up your skills and warehouse. On your personal island, you can also open a Specialty Workshop that produces items more efficiently than in the port and does not consume regular crafting time (though it does use the island's internal resources).

To interact with another player, click their nickname in-game [Ctrl], in chat, or from the Friends or Guild Members lists. You can trade with any other players at sea by sailing up to each other and using the social menu. Tradeable resources must be in the hold. While in a fleet (even with captured ships) or in the arena, you can send quick messages. The default key is [Z].
